topics.title: US forces capture Maduro; the Monroe Doctrine returns
topics.hook: US forces raided Caracas on 3 January 2026 and flew President Nicolas Maduro to New York on narcoterrorism charges, and Washington's oldest claim on Latin America is back in play.
topics.story:
In the early hours of 3 January 2026, US special forces raided Caracas and captured Nicolas Maduro, Venezuela's president since 2013, along with his wife Cilia Flores. Both were flown to the United States and taken to a federal detention centre in New York, where Maduro faces charges of narcoterrorism and conspiracy to import cocaine. Venezuelan officials said a large part of Maduro's security detail was killed in the raid; Cuba's government said 32 Cuban personnel died fighting alongside Maduro's forces.

President Trump called the operation one of the most "stunning, effective and powerful displays of American military might" in the country's history and said the US would "run" Venezuela until a "safe, proper and judicious transition" could be arranged. On 5 January, Vice President Delcy Rodriguez was sworn in as interim president before the National Assembly. Her government began releasing political prisoners on 8 January.

The episode is being read through the Monroe Doctrine of 1823, in which President James Monroe told Congress that European powers should not interfere in the Americas and that the US would treat any such interference as a threat to its own peace and safety. The doctrine was never a law; it was a unilateral claim of a sphere of influence, later stretched by the Roosevelt Corollary of 1904 to justify US intervention within Latin America itself, not just against outside powers. Grenada in 1983 and Panama in 1989 — where US forces captured General Manuel Noriega on drug charges, a close parallel to the Maduro operation — are the template this raid follows.

Venezuela calls itself the Bolivarian Republic, a name adopted in 1999 under Hugo Chavez in honour of Simon Bolivar, the independence leader who liberated six South American nations from Spanish rule. Chavez's "Bolivarian Revolution" combined anti-US rhetoric with oil wealth; he died in 2013 and Maduro succeeded him. The US had already tried unseating Maduro once, recognising opposition leader Juan Guaido as interim president in 2019 — an effort that fizzled. Washington has run sanctions on Venezuela's oil sector since 2017.

Venezuela holds the world's largest proven crude oil reserves and was a founding member of OPEC in 1960. It is also a member of the Organization of American States, the regional body headquartered in Washington DC since 1948, though Venezuela withdrew from the OAS in 2019 during the Guaido standoff. Critics of the raid point to Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, which bars the use of force against a state's territorial integrity or political independence, as the raid's central legal problem — a charge the US has not directly answered.

For CLAT, the durable trivia sits in named doctrines and dated founding moments: 1823 for Monroe, 1904 for the Roosevelt Corollary, 1960 for OPEC, 1948 for the OAS, 1999 for the Bolivarian renaming. The current-affairs layer — Maduro's capture, Rodriguez's swearing-in, the Cuban casualties — supplies the date-specific questions; the static layer supplies the trap options examiners like to plant beside them.

topics.title: EU's Costa and von der Leyen become Republic Day's first joint chief guests
topics.hook: For the first time in 77 years of Republic Day, the chief guests were not a country but the European Union, represented by two presidents, and the visit doubled as the 16th India-EU Summit.
topics.story:
European Council President Antonio Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen were the chief guests at India's 77th Republic Day parade on 26 January 2026, the first time the EU as a bloc — rather than a country or its head of state — has held that slot. Their three-day state visit, from 25 to 27 January, doubled as the 16th India-EU Summit, hosted in New Delhi and co-chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Republic Day marks the date the Constitution of India came into force: 26 January 1950, chosen because the Indian National Congress had observed 26 January 1930 as Purna Swaraj (complete independence) day. The chief guest tradition began in 1950 itself, when Indonesian President Sukarno attended. Guests have ranged from Cold War-era leaders to, in 2018, all ten ASEAN heads of state and government simultaneously — the only other year the slot went to multiple leaders. France's presidents have been invited the most times of any single country.

The EU is not a state; it is a supranational union of 27 member countries, built on the Maastricht Treaty of 1992, which created the EU from the earlier European Economic Community (established 1957 by the Treaty of Rome). It has its own Parliament, Commission, and Council, and — since the Lisbon Treaty of 2009 — a European Council President who chairs summits of national leaders, a post now held by Costa. Von der Leyen, as European Commission President, heads the EU's executive branch, comparable loosely to India's Council of Ministers.

The summit's headline outcome was progress on the India-EU Free Trade Agreement, under negotiation since 2007 and still incomplete, alongside a joint statement on connectivity, technology, and security cooperation. Both sides also renewed calls for reform of the UN Security Council. On 21 January, days before the summit, India's envoy spoke on behalf of the G4 — Brazil, Germany, India, and Japan, a grouping that has jointly pushed for permanent Security Council seats since 2004 — at an Intergovernmental Negotiations meeting in New York. The Security Council currently has five permanent members (US, UK, France, Russia, China) holding veto power under Article 27 of the UN Charter, plus ten non-permanent members elected for two-year terms; India has never held a permanent seat despite being the world's most populous country.

For an exam, the layered facts are what matter: the constitutional date of 26 January 1950, the Purna Swaraj precedent of 1930, the EU's own founding treaties, and the G4's stated goal against the five veto-holding P5 members. The 2026 chief guest slot is unusual enough — a bloc, not a nation — that expect at least one question testing whether students know it broke the single-leader convention.

topics.title: India takes over the BRICS chair for 2026
topics.hook: India became BRICS chair on 1 January 2026, its fourth turn at the helm, and this time it must steer a bloc of ten members instead of the original five.
topics.story:
India assumed the BRICS chairmanship on 1 January 2026 under the theme "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability," and will host the 18th BRICS Summit later in the year. It is India's fourth BRICS presidency; the earlier three came in 2012, 2016 and 2021.

BRICS began as an acronym coined in 2001 by Goldman Sachs economist Jim O'Neill, grouping Brazil, Russia, India and China as fast-growing emerging economies. The four held their first formal summit in 2009 in Yekaterinburg, Russia. South Africa joined in 2010, turning BRIC into BRICS. The bloc expanded sharply at its 2023 Johannesburg summit, admitting Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE (Saudi Arabia has not formally taken up membership), and Indonesia joined in January 2025 — making this the first Indian presidency of the expanded, ten-member group.

BRICS has built two concrete institutions since 2014: the New Development Bank, headquartered in Shanghai, which finances infrastructure and sustainable development projects in member and partner countries, and the Contingent Reserve Arrangement, a $100 billion currency-swap mechanism meant to help members handle balance-of-payments pressure without turning to the IMF. Both emerged from the 2014 Fortaleza Summit in Brazil.

The bloc has no binding charter or permanent secretariat; it runs on annual rotating chairs and consensus, which is both its flexibility and its weakness — India will need to hold together members with sharply different positions on Russia's war in Ukraine, Iran's nuclear standoff with the West, and China's trade posture. BRICS members collectively account for a large share of world population and a growing share of global GDP by purchasing power parity, which is the statistic supporters cite most often to argue the bloc is displacing the G7 as the more representative grouping of the world economy.

For CLAT, treat this as a scaffolding topic: BRICS's founding year as an acronym (2001) versus its first actual summit (2009) is a classic trap, as is confusing the New Development Bank with the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, a separate China-led institution headquartered in Beijing since 2016.

topics.title: Supreme Court: no customs duty on electricity from SEZ to DTA
topics.hook: The Supreme Court ruled on 5 January 2026 that electricity generated inside a Special Economic Zone and sold outside it cannot be taxed as if it were an imported good.
topics.story:
On 5 January 2026, the Supreme Court decided Adani Power Ltd. v. Union of India, holding that customs duty cannot be levied on electricity generated in a Special Economic Zone and supplied to the Domestic Tariff Area — the ordinary, non-SEZ part of the country. The bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and N V Anjaria set aside a 2019 Gujarat High Court ruling that had gone the other way, and ordered a refund, without interest, of duty Adani Power had paid under protest between September 2010 and February 2016.

The case turned on how SEZ law treats the boundary between an SEZ and the rest of India. Under the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005, an SEZ is legally deemed to be foreign territory for trade and duty purposes — goods moving from an SEZ into the Domestic Tariff Area are treated like imports, attracting customs duty under the Customs Act, 1962. The Gujarat High Court had applied that logic to electricity too. The Supreme Court disagreed: it held that customs duty can only be levied under the authority of a validly issued notification, and found the relevant government notifications did not, in fact, extend to electrical energy in the way the tax authorities claimed. Without that specific legal authorisation, the demand violated Article 265 of the Constitution, which says no tax can be levied or collected except by authority of law.

SEZs themselves date to India's SEZ policy of 2000, formalised by the 2005 Act, meant to boost exports by offering duty exemptions, tax holidays and simplified customs procedures inside designated zones. Adani Power's SEZ unit, at the centre of this case, generates electricity that it also supplies outside the zone — a common arrangement questioned repeatedly by tax authorities across sectors, not just power.

The ruling matters beyond one company's refund. It reinforces a doctrine central to Indian tax law: that taxation is a creature of statute, and courts will not stretch a notification's language to cover a levy the executive wants but never explicitly authorised. It sits alongside a separate January 2026 Supreme Court ruling — decided the same month — that the executive cannot retain money collected under a levy imposed without legal authority, a related application of Article 265's "no taxation without law" principle to a different set of facts.

For CLAT, remember Article 265 as the anchor provision, and be ready to distinguish it from Article 266 (Consolidated Fund) and Article 270 (distribution of tax revenue between the Centre and states) — three articles examiners like to bundle into one taxation-themed question.

topics.title: Supreme Court reads menstrual health into Article 21
topics.hook: The Supreme Court held that the right to life under Article 21 includes a right to menstrual health, pushing sanitary pad access and dignity for menstruating students into the language of fundamental rights.
topics.story:
In January 2026, the Supreme Court held that the right to life and personal liberty guaranteed by Article 21 of the Constitution extends to menstrual health — access to sanitary products, sanitation facilities, and freedom from stigma around menstruation, particularly for girls in schools. The ruling responded to petitions flagging poor sanitation infrastructure and irregular sanitary pad distribution in government schools, especially in rural areas, where absenteeism among menstruating students is a documented driver of girls dropping out.

Article 21's text is spare — "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law" — but the Supreme Court has spent decades reading it expansively. The turning point was Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), which held that "procedure established by law" must itself be fair, just and reasonable, effectively importing due process into Indian constitutional law. Since then, the Court has folded in the right to a clean environment (Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar, 1991), the right to health (Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India, 1984), the right to privacy (K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India, 2017, a nine-judge bench), and the right to a dignified death (Common Cause v. Union of India, 2018). The menstrual health ruling continues that pattern, treating a specific, previously unstated need as an inseparable part of a dignified life.

The government's response predates the judgment: the Menstrual Hygiene Scheme, run by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, has distributed subsidised sanitary napkins through Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs) since 2011, and several states run their own free-pad programmes in schools. The Court's ruling gives these schemes constitutional weight — they are no longer only policy choices but implementations of a fundamental right, which changes how courts will treat future cuts or gaps in provision.

The same month, the Court also stayed contested UGC regulations in a separate matter, a reminder that January 2026 was an unusually dense month for Article 21-adjacent rulings. For CLAT, the menstrual health case is best understood as one entry in a long chain of judgments that keep widening Article 21 without amending its text — a pattern examiners test by asking which right came from which case, and in what year.

topics.title: Padma Awards 2026: 131 honoured, Dharmendra and V.S. Achuthanandan among posthumous picks
topics.hook: The government named 131 Padma Award winners on the eve of Republic Day 2026, including five Padma Vibhushans, two of them awarded posthumously.
topics.story:
The Padma Awards 2026 were announced on 25 January, the eve of Republic Day, honouring 131 people: 5 Padma Vibhushan, 13 Padma Bhushan and 113 Padma Shri recipients. Nineteen women were honoured and 16 awards were conferred posthumously. President Droupadi Murmu formally approved the list; the investiture ceremony followed later in the year, at Rashtrapati Bhavan.

The Padma Vibhushan, India's second-highest civilian award, went posthumously to actor Dharmendra and to V.S. Achuthanandan, a former Kerala chief minister and veteran CPI(M) leader. The Padma Bhushan, the third tier, went to Malayalam superstar Mammootty and playback singer Alka Yagnik, among others. At the Padma Shri level, actors R. Madhavan and Prosenjit Chatterjee were honoured alongside cricket captains Rohit Sharma and Harmanpreet Kaur, both recognised for leading India to World Cup titles.

The three Padma awards sit below the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian honour, in a four-tier system that has run — with one interruption between 1977 and 1980, when the awards were briefly discontinued — since 1954. Selection runs through a Padma Awards Committee, constituted each year by the Prime Minister, which examines nominations submitted online and recommends names to the President. The awards recognise "distinguished and exceptional achievement" in fields including arts, literature, science, public affairs, medicine, social work, sports and trade and industry — a list broader than most civilian honour systems worldwide, which tend to separate arts and public-service honours entirely.

The Bharat Ratna, by contrast, is reserved for the very highest achievement and has gone unawarded in many years; recent recipients (2024) include Karpoori Thakur, Lal Krishna Advani, M.S. Swaminathan, Chaudhary Charan Singh and P.V. Narasimha Rao — the first time five people received it in a single year. No Bharat Ratna was announced alongside the 2026 Padma list.

For CLAT, the numbers matter more than the names: the exact count of 131, the 5-13-113 split across the three tiers, and the constitutional-adjacent trivia that these are not "titles" in the Article 18 sense — the Supreme Court settled in Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1996) that Padma and Bharat Ratna awards do not violate Article 18's ban on titles, since they carry no automatic prefix like "Sir" or "Rai Bahadur" once did.

topics.title: Gaza ceasefire enters phase two as the last hostage body is recovered
topics.hook: The US declared phase two of its Gaza ceasefire plan on 16 January 2026, even as monitors counted over a thousand violations of the deal struck three months earlier.
topics.story:
The United States declared the start of phase two of the Gaza ceasefire on 16 January 2026, under the "Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict" that Israel and Hamas had first accepted on 8 October 2025. The plan's earlier phase had already produced the return of all living hostages and, gradually, the recovery of the bodies of the dead; the last of the 28 deceased Israeli hostages, Ran Gvili, was recovered on 26 January 2026.

Compliance with the ceasefire's first phase was contested throughout. Gaza's Government Media Office recorded at least 1,193 Israeli violations between 10 October 2025 and 9 January 2026 — strikes, artillery fire and direct shootings — and Al Jazeera's own tally found attacks reported on 82 of the first 97 days of the truce, meaning only 15 days passed without violence. Humanitarian access lagged too: of roughly 54,000 aid trucks the plan envisaged entering Gaza, only about 23,019 had crossed by 9 January, an average of 255 trucks a day against a target far higher.

The war that produced this ceasefire began on 7 October 2023, when Hamas fighters crossed from Gaza into southern Israel, killed roughly 1,200 people and took about 250 hostage — the deadliest single day for Jews since the Holocaust. Israel's military response over the following two years killed tens of thousands of Palestinians in Gaza, according to Gaza's health ministry, and displaced most of the territory's population. The current plan traces to a framework the Trump administration pushed through 2025, building on years of failed truces brokered separately by Egypt, Qatar and the US.

Gaza has been governed separately from the West Bank since Hamas won Palestinian legislative elections in 2006 and then took full control of the Strip in 2007, splitting Palestinian governance between Hamas in Gaza and the Fatah-led Palestinian Authority in the West Bank — a division that complicates any "day after" plan for Gaza's post-war administration, since no single Palestinian body currently controls both territories.

For CLAT, keep the war's start date (7 October 2023) and the ceasefire's start date (8 October 2025) distinct — two years apart almost to the day — since exam-setters like pairing dates that are easy to conflate.

topics.title: Russia, Ukraine and the US hold peace talks in Abu Dhabi
topics.hook: Ukrainian, Russian and American negotiators met in Abu Dhabi on 23-24 January 2026 for talks officials called '90 percent' of the way to a peace deal, with territory and a nuclear plant the last sticking points.
topics.story:
Russia, Ukraine and the United States held talks in Abu Dhabi on 23-24 January 2026, working from a draft peace plan the Trump administration had circulated. The discussions covered disengagement of forces, ceasefire monitoring, and a prisoner exchange involving 314 people. Trump had already pushed through a one-week "energy ceasefire" to build momentum, and European, American and Ukrainian officials described the broader agreement as roughly 90 percent complete — though the Kremlin's own position remained further from the draft than that figure suggested.

On 27 January, Ukraine's foreign minister said President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was willing to meet Vladimir Putin directly to resolve the two hardest unresolved issues: territorial control and the fate of the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, Europe's largest, which Russian forces have occupied since March 2022 and which has repeatedly lost outside power amid fighting nearby.

The war began with Russia's full-scale invasion on 24 February 2022, following eight years of lower-intensity conflict in eastern Ukraine's Donbas region that started after Russia annexed Crimea in 2014. The Abu Dhabi round built on earlier December 2025 talks in Florida and a January 2026 round in Paris — a sequence showing how many capitals had by then become involved in brokering an end to Europe's largest land war since 1945.

Abu Dhabi's choice as a venue reflects the United Arab Emirates' position as a rare state maintaining working relationships with Moscow, Kyiv and Washington simultaneously, a role it has played in earlier prisoner exchanges during the war. Zaporizhzhia itself is significant beyond the immediate conflict: it is one of the ten largest nuclear plants in the world by reactor count, and its status — whether it returns to Ukrainian control, stays under Russian occupation, or moves to some international administration — will likely shape how the eventual territorial settlement is drawn.

For CLAT, keep the invasion's start date (24 February 2022) distinct from the earlier Crimea annexation (2014), since exam questions frequently test whether students can place these two escalations correctly on a single timeline.

topics.title: RBI cuts the repo rate as growth outpaces inflation
topics.hook: The Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Policy Committee cut the repo rate in its first meeting of 2026, choosing to back growth running near 8 percent over a hawkish stance on inflation that has already cooled sharply.
topics.story:
The RBI's Monetary Policy Committee cut the repo rate by 25 basis points at its January 2026 meeting, continuing a downward move that reflects India's growth running near 8.2 percent even as headline inflation has fallen to around 1.7 percent — well below the RBI's own comfort zone. The MPC is a six-member body created by a 2016 amendment to the RBI Act, 1934, with three members from the RBI and three external appointees, chaired by the RBI Governor. It targets consumer price inflation of 4 percent, with a tolerance band of plus-or-minus 2 percent, a framework known as flexible inflation targeting adopted in 2016 under a formal agreement between the RBI and the central government.

The repo rate is the rate at which the RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks against government securities; cutting it makes borrowing cheaper across the economy, in theory nudging banks to lower lending rates for consumers and businesses. Its mirror, the reverse repo rate, is what the RBI pays banks for parking surplus funds with it overnight — currently less central to policy signalling than the repo rate and the Standing Deposit Facility, introduced in 2022.

The RBI's own commentary framed the January cut as a deliberate shift from rigid inflation targeting toward prioritising growth, an argument that low and falling inflation gives room to support demand without stoking prices. This marks a departure from the RBI's more cautious stance through much of 2023 and 2024, when repo rates were held steady at higher levels to guard against inflation shocks from global oil prices and supply disruptions.

Monetary policy sits constitutionally and statutorily distinct from fiscal policy, which is the government's domain through the Union Budget — Nirmala Sitharaman's ninth consecutive budget as Finance Minister was due days after this MPC meeting, on 1 February 2026, and commentators expected fiscal and monetary policy to move in the same growth-supportive direction that month.

For CLAT, remember the numbers precisely: repo rate is a bank-borrowing-cost tool, the RBI Act is from 1934, the MPC's inflation target is 4 percent with a 2 percent band, and the MPC framework itself is an amendment from 2016 — four distinct facts examiners often scramble across multiple-choice options.

topics.title: China's live-fire drills push closer to Taiwan than ever
topics.hook: Chinese rockets landed within Taiwan's 24-nautical-mile contiguous zone during live-fire drills over the New Year, the closest Beijing has fired to the island since 2022.
topics.story:
China's military ran large-scale exercises simulating a blockade of Taiwan from 29-30 December 2025 into the new year, under the name Justice Mission 2025 — the second such exercise in 2025. Taiwan's defence ministry said the People's Liberation Army fired 27 rockets during the drills, of which 10 landed within Taiwan's 24-nautical-mile contiguous zone, the closest Chinese live-fire activity to the island since 2022, when Beijing last staged comparably aggressive drills after then-US House Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

The US State Department said China's military activity and rhetoric toward Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines were raising tensions "unnecessarily" and called for meaningful dialogue instead. Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te responded by vowing to defend the island's sovereignty and increase defence spending, continuing a posture he has held since taking office in 2024. Through January, analysts tracking the region described China running a "dual-track" approach: escalating military and diplomatic pressure on Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines while simultaneously deepening economic and security ties with South and Southeast Asian partners.

The dispute traces to 1949, when the Chinese Civil War ended with the Communist Party controlling the mainland as the People's Republic of China and the defeated Nationalist government retreating to Taiwan, which it has governed separately ever since. Beijing considers Taiwan a breakaway province that must eventually reunify with the mainland, by force if necessary, and rejects any move toward formal Taiwanese independence. The United States maintains a policy of "strategic ambiguity" under the Taiwan Relations Act of 1979, supplying Taiwan with defensive weapons without formally committing to defend it militarily, while officially recognising only the "One China" position without endorsing Beijing's claim outright.

Taiwan's contiguous zone — the 24-nautical-mile band beyond its 12-nautical-mile territorial sea — is a concept from the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), 1982, within which a coastal state can enforce customs, fiscal, immigration and sanitary laws, though it falls short of full territorial sovereignty. Chinese rockets landing inside that zone, rather than in Taiwan's territorial waters proper, is calibrated brinkmanship: provocative without crossing the line into an act most governments would call a direct territorial violation.

For CLAT, the useful anchor is 1949 for the civil war's end and the "One China" policy's origin, alongside the Taiwan Relations Act of 1979 as the specific US law governing its unofficial support for Taiwan — a pairing exam-setters often test together.

topics.title: ISRO's first launch of 2026 fails to reach orbit
topics.hook: ISRO's PSLV-C62, carrying a DRDO earth-observation satellite and 15 co-passenger payloads, lifted off on 12 January 2026 but failed to reach orbit — a rare setback for India's most reliable launch vehicle.
topics.story:
ISRO launched the PSLV-C62 mission from Sriharikota on 12 January 2026, its first orbital launch attempt of the year and the 101st orbital launch in the organisation's history. The primary payload was EOS-N1, code-named Anvesha, a next-generation earth-observation satellite developed jointly with the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO). Fifteen co-passenger satellites rode alongside it, including seven from the Hyderabad-based private company Dhruva Space — the first time a single Indian private firm had contributed that many satellites to one PSLV mission. The launch failed to place its payloads in orbit.

The Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle, ISRO's workhorse since its first successful flight in 1994, has built a reputation as one of the most reliable rockets in the world, with a long run of consecutive successful launches carrying everything from India's own satellites to commercial payloads for other countries. It was a PSLV that carried Chandrayaan-1 in 2008 and Mangalyaan, India's Mars Orbiter Mission, in 2013 — the latter making India the first country to reach Mars orbit on its first attempt, and the first Asian nation to reach Mars at all.

ISRO's broader 2026 calendar was built around a busy schedule: agency officials had said before the launch that ISRO planned seven satellite missions by March 2026, of which PSLV-C62 was the first. Failures are rare enough for the PSLV that each one draws close scrutiny — ISRO typically convenes a failure analysis committee to trace the fault before its next launch, a process that delayed missions for months after the PSLV-C39 anomaly in 2017, one of the vehicle's few earlier failures.

DRDO's involvement in EOS-N1 reflects a growing pattern of India's defence and space establishments collaborating on dual-use earth-observation satellites, which serve both civilian mapping and military surveillance purposes — a category distinct from India's dedicated military satellites like the GSAT series and the RISAT radar-imaging satellites.

For CLAT, the reliable trivia is structural: PSLV's first flight (1994), its role in Chandrayaan-1 (2008) and Mangalyaan (2013), and India's status as the first nation to reach Mars orbit on a maiden attempt — facts that outlast any single mission's outcome, including this failure.

topics.title: Davos 2026 convenes under 'A Spirit of Dialogue' as risk report flags misinformation
topics.hook: The World Economic Forum's 56th Annual Meeting ran in Davos from 19-23 January 2026, opening with a Global Risks Report that ranked misinformation the top short-term threat to the world for a second year running.
topics.story:
The World Economic Forum held its 56th Annual Meeting in Davos, Switzerland, from 19 to 23 January 2026, under the theme "A Spirit of Dialogue." Discussions organised around five themes: cooperation in a contested world, unlocking new sources of growth, investing in people, deploying innovation responsibly, and building prosperity within planetary boundaries.

The Forum's Global Risks Report 2026, released ahead of the meeting, ranked misinformation and disinformation as the top global risk over a two-year horizon for the second consecutive year, ahead of extreme weather events, societal polarisation, and geoeconomic confrontation. Over a longer ten-year horizon, the report placed extreme weather and other climate-linked risks higher. The report specifically flagged how generative AI has lowered the cost of producing convincing false content, citing elections in the US, India, Pakistan, Japan, Ireland, the Netherlands and Argentina as having already been affected by fabricated material aimed at discrediting candidates.

The WEF itself was founded in 1971 by Klaus Schwab, a German engineer and economist, initially as the "European Management Forum" before renaming itself the World Economic Forum in 1987. It is a Swiss non-profit foundation, not an intergovernmental body — a distinction students often miss, since Davos's guest list of heads of state and central bank governors makes it feel governmental. Its annual meeting in the Swiss ski town of Davos has run most years since 1971, interrupted occasionally by crises like the pandemic, which forced a virtual 2021 meeting and a rescheduled, delayed 2022 edition held in May rather than January.

Beyond the risk report, Davos 2026 drew record attendance from world leaders, according to the WEF's own framing, reflecting how central the forum has become as an informal venue for sideline diplomacy even though it has no negotiating or treaty-making authority of its own — decisions made there are non-binding, unlike outcomes at UN or G20 summits.

For CLAT, the useful hooks are the WEF's founding year (1971) and founder (Klaus Schwab), its private, non-intergovernmental character, and the specific risk hierarchy — misinformation topping the near-term list while climate risk dominates the decade-long outlook — since exam questions sometimes test whether students can distinguish short-term versus long-term risk rankings within the same report.

topics.title: Parliament's Budget Session 2026 convenes
topics.hook: Parliament's Budget Session opened on 28 January 2026, days before Nirmala Sitharaman's ninth straight Budget, which for the first time in Indian history fell on a Sunday.
topics.story:
Parliament's Budget Session 2026 began on 28 January, opening — as every Budget Session does — with the President's address to a joint sitting of both Houses under Article 87 of the Constitution, followed by the Economic Survey, tabled by the Finance Ministry a day or two before the Budget itself. The Union Budget followed on 1 February, presented by Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman for the ninth consecutive year since 2019, and for the first time ever on a Sunday.

The Budget Session is traditionally split into two parts with a recess in between, during which department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees examine budget proposals in detail — a structure meant to give MPs more scrutiny time than a single continuous sitting would allow. Article 112 requires the government to lay an "Annual Financial Statement" — the formal constitutional name for what is popularly called the Union Budget — before Parliament each year, estimating receipts and expenditure for the coming financial year.

During this session, both Houses together passed nine bills and returned another nine, with one bill withdrawn in the Lok Sabha, a fairly typical Budget Session legislative haul. The Finance Bill, which gives legal effect to the Budget's taxation proposals, is traditionally passed later in the session, after the general discussion on the Budget concludes and ministries' individual demands for grants are voted on.

For CLAT, know Article 112 as the Budget's constitutional name-check, and Article 87 for the President's address — two provisions frequently tested together since students conflate "the Budget" as a term with any specific constitutional article name.

topics.title: Supreme Court splits on Prevention of Corruption Act sanction requirement
topics.hook: A Supreme Court bench delivered a split verdict in January 2026 on whether prior government approval is constitutionally required before investigating a public servant for corruption.
topics.story:
The Supreme Court delivered a split verdict in January 2026 on the constitutional validity of requiring prior approval before investigating a public servant under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. The requirement — inserted as Section 17A by a 2018 amendment to the Act — mandates that investigating agencies obtain approval from the relevant government authority before even opening a probe into decisions or recommendations a public servant made in an official capacity.

Supporters of Section 17A argue it protects honest officials from being harassed with investigations over bona fide decisions that later turn out badly, encouraging bureaucrats to take decisions without fear. Critics argue it hands the executive a veto over whether its own officials get investigated at all, undermining the independence corruption investigations need to function, and that it effectively delays or blocks probes into politically connected individuals.

A split verdict means the two (or more) judges on the bench disagreed and the matter typically goes to a larger bench for a final resolution — a procedural outcome distinct from a "dissenting opinion," which is when a minority judge disagrees but the majority's view still becomes binding law.

For CLAT, know Section 17A's insertion year (2018) and be ready to distinguish a split verdict, which leaves the underlying question legally unsettled, from a majority judgment with dissent, which does settle it.

topics.title: AM Green's Kakinada plant hits equipment milestone, signs Uniper deal
topics.hook: India's first mega green ammonia project, coming up at Kakinada, reached a major construction milestone in January 2026 and signed a long-term supply deal with Germany's Uniper.
topics.story:
Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu and Deputy CM Pawan Kalyan attended the First Major Equipment Erection Ceremony at AM Green's Kakinada green ammonia and green hydrogen plant in mid-January 2026, marking a construction milestone for what is billed as India's first commercial-scale project of its kind. The plant, being built on a 495-acre site by transforming an existing ammonia-urea facility, targets 1.5 million tonnes of green ammonia annually once fully operational from June 2027, with an investment of roughly Rs 13,000 crore and over 2,500 jobs expected.

In January 2026, AM Green also signed a long-term offtake agreement with Uniper, Germany's energy major, to supply up to 500,000 tonnes a year of RFNBO-compliant ammonia (ammonia certified as a "Renewable Fuel of Non-Biological Origin" under EU rules) from 2028, with most of Kakinada's output ultimately headed for Germany.

Green ammonia is made by combining green hydrogen — hydrogen produced via electrolysis powered by renewable electricity, rather than from fossil fuels — with nitrogen extracted from the air, avoiding the carbon emissions of conventional ammonia production, which is otherwise one of the most carbon-intensive industrial processes in the world. Ammonia itself is a key input for fertiliser and a candidate marine and industrial fuel, giving projects like Kakinada relevance well beyond the chemicals sector.

For CLAT, retain the numbers: 1.5 million tonnes annual capacity, June 2027 production start, and the RFNBO certification standard, since environment and economy questions often test whether students can define a technical export standard correctly rather than just recall the project's existence.

topics.title: Bangladesh heads toward a February election amid strained India ties
topics.hook: With Bangladesh's general election set for February 2026, India-Bangladesh relations were unusually tense through January, unsettled by the fallout from Sheikh Hasina's 2024 ouster.
topics.story:
Bangladesh's politics remained tense through January 2026 as the country prepared for general elections in February, its first since a mass uprising forced Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina to flee to India in August 2024, ending her 15-year rule. India-Bangladesh relations stayed strained over India's continued hosting of Hasina, whom Dhaka's interim authorities want extradited to face charges, alongside friction over cricket ties and broader questions about the shape of the post-Hasina political order.

Hasina's Awami League, which had governed Bangladesh for most of the previous two decades, faced disqualification questions ahead of the vote, opening space for older parties like the Bangladesh Nationalist Party and newer forces such as the National Citizens Party, formed by leaders of the 2024 student movement, to compete for a rebuilt political landscape. Bangladesh's 1971 Liberation War, in which India intervened militarily to help create an independent Bangladesh out of what was then East Pakistan, remains the deepest historical layer beneath the current relationship — a bond of shared origin now complicated by the asylum dispute.

For CLAT, connect this to South Asia's pattern of executive transitions via street protest rather than the ballot box in 2024-25 — Bangladesh and Sri Lanka both saw leaders removed this way — since comparative-regional questions often test whether students can place several such episodes on one timeline.

topics.title: Nepal's Gen Z-protest transition heads toward a March election
topics.hook: Months after Nepal's Gen Z protests toppled its government, former Prime Minister K.P. Sharma Oli gave testimony to an inquiry probing the deadly crackdown, as the country moved toward March 2026 elections.
topics.story:
Nepal continued working through the aftermath of its September 2025 "Gen Z protests" through January 2026. The demonstrations, organised rapidly through mobile phones and social media, forced the resignation of Prime Minister K.P. Sharma Oli's government within days of starting. In January, Oli gave a written statement to a government inquiry commission investigating a deadly crackdown on protesters during the unrest.

The protest movement fed into the two-year-old Rashtriya Swatantra Party (RSP), a relatively new political force that absorbed much of the organisational energy of the student-led uprising, positioning it to contest fresh elections scheduled for March 2026 — just six months after the government's fall, an unusually compressed transition timeline by regional standards.

Nepal became a federal democratic republic in 2008, when its Constituent Assembly abolished the 240-year-old Shah monarchy, ending a political transition that had begun with the 2006 people's movement against King Gyanendra's direct rule. The 2025 protests are best read as a second major youth-driven upheaval in Nepal's short republican history, testing whether its democratic institutions can absorb this kind of shock without another prolonged constitutional crisis.

For CLAT, note Nepal's monarchy abolition year (2008) as the anchor static fact, with the 2025 Gen Z protests as the current-affairs layer testing whether that republican settlement is holding.

topics.title: Sudan's civil war deepens in Darfur
topics.hook: Civilian deaths and mass displacement kept mounting in Sudan's Darfur region through January 2026, as the Rapid Support Forces rejected a ceasefire proposal backed by the UN and African Union.
topics.story:
Sudan's civil war, now in its third year, continued to worsen in Darfur through January 2026. At least 19 civilians were killed in a ground assault in North Darfur's Jarjira area, and 10 more died in a drone attack on Sinja in Sennar state; the International Organization for Migration estimated more than 8,000 people fled villages in North Darfur's Kernoi locality in early January alone, some crossing into Chad.

The war began in April 2023 as a power struggle between Sudan's regular army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), two factions that had earlier cooperated in the 2021 military coup that derailed Sudan's transition to civilian rule following the 2019 overthrow of long-time ruler Omar al-Bashir. Sudan's transitional prime minister proposed an immediate ceasefire in December 2025, monitored by the UN, African Union and the League of Arab States, including a full RSF withdrawal from territory it controls — a plan the RSF rejected.

The International Criminal Court has confirmed evidence of war crimes and crimes against humanity committed by the RSF in El Fasher, Darfur's largest city, adding a layer of international accountability to a conflict that has otherwise drawn less sustained global attention than Gaza, Ukraine or Venezuela.

For CLAT, keep the war's start (April 2023) and the earlier coup (2021) distinct — two separate crises three years apart that examiners occasionally merge into one date.

topics.title: Alcaraz completes the career Grand Slam at the Australian Open
topics.hook: Carlos Alcaraz beat Novak Djokovic in the 2026 Australian Open final to complete a career Grand Slam at 22, the youngest man to do so in the Open Era's recent history.
topics.story:
Carlos Alcaraz defeated Novak Djokovic 2-6, 6-2, 6-3, 7-5 in the men's singles final of the 2026 Australian Open, his first title at Melbourne Park and seventh Grand Slam overall. The win completed his career Grand Slam — winning all four majors (Australian Open, French Open, Wimbledon, US Open) at least once — making him the ninth man in tennis history to achieve it and, at 22 years, 8 months and 27 days, the youngest to do so.

In the women's draw, Elena Rybakina beat Aryna Sabalenka 6-4, 4-6, 6-4 for her second Grand Slam title. The Australian Open, first held in 1905 and one of the sport's four majors alongside Wimbledon (the oldest, from 1877), the French Open (from 1891) and the US Open (from 1881), is played on hard courts at Melbourne Park.

The "career Grand Slam" is distinct from a single-season "Grand Slam" — winning all four majors in the same calendar year, achieved by only a handful of players in the Open Era, most recently by no one on the men's side since Rod Laver in 1969.

For CLAT, keep career Grand Slam (all four majors across a career) and calendar Grand Slam (all four in one year) as clearly separate concepts, since sports-trivia questions frequently blur the two.

topics.title: Milan Cortina 2026 torch relay reaches Cortina, 70 years after 1956
topics.hook: The Olympic flame reached Cortina d'Ampezzo on 26 January 2026, seventy years after the town last hosted the Winter Games in 1956, ahead of the Milan-Cortina Games opening on 6 February.
topics.story:
The Milan Cortina 2026 Olympic torch relay, carrying 10,001 torchbearers across roughly 12,000 kilometres from 26 November 2025 to 6 February 2026, reached Cortina d'Ampezzo on 26 January 2026 — exactly seventy years after the town hosted the 1956 Winter Olympics, the last time Italy staged the Winter Games before this edition. Along the way, the relay crossed Genoa on 9 January, traversed the Lombard lake district on 14-15 January, and travelled by gondola along Venice's Grand Canal on 22 January.

Milan and Cortina d'Ampezzo are co-hosting the 2026 Winter Olympics, the first Winter Games split across two host cities in Italy and only the third time in Olympic history the Winter Games have had multiple host cities in different regions. The torch itself, designed by Carlo Ratti Associati, is a 1,060-gram flute of recycled aluminium running on renewable liquefied petroleum gas — a deliberate sustainability choice for a Games that has marketed itself around reduced environmental impact.

For CLAT, the useful anchor is 1956 as Italy's only prior Winter Olympics host year (Cortina alone, that time), a fact likely to appear as a distractor option in any Winter Olympics history question through 2026.

topics.title: The Supreme Court tightens the 25% school quota
topics.hook: A private school that takes no state money still has to keep a quarter of its entry class for children it did not choose.
topics.story:
The Supreme Court strengthened enforcement of the **25% reservation** for children from weaker sections and disadvantaged groups in **private unaided schools**, directing states to frame rules through consultation and to fix the reimbursement question that has stalled compliance for a decade.

The obligation comes from **Section 12(1)(c)** of the **Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009**, which requires unaided schools to admit at least a quarter of their entry-level class from those categories and provide free elementary education to them. The state reimburses the school at its own per-child expenditure or the school's fee, whichever is lower, which is where the disputes begin, because the reimbursement rate is usually well below the fee.

The Act itself follows **Article 21A**, inserted by the **Eighty-Sixth Amendment in 2002**, which makes free and compulsory education for children aged **six to fourteen** a fundamental right. The same amendment moved the old **Article 45** to cover early childhood care below six and added **Article 51A(k)**, a fundamental duty on parents to provide education.

The constitutionality of Section 12(1)(c) was upheld in **Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan v. Union of India (2012)**, with the Court exempting unaided **minority** institutions from the obligation, reasoning that **Article 30(1)** protects their right to administer. **Pramati Educational Trust (2014)** confirmed that exemption for both aided and unaided minority schools, which is why the quota reaches only a part of the private sector.

topics.title: Who may investigate a judge, and why none has ever been removed
topics.hook: The Constitution calls it removal, not impeachment, and in seventy-five years it has never been completed.
topics.story:
The Supreme Court clarified the **Speaker's authority** to constitute an inquiry committee into allegations against a judge, and noted that no judge of a High Court or the Supreme Court has ever actually been removed.

The procedure sits in **Article 124(4)**, applied to High Court judges by **Article 217(1)(b)**. A judge may be removed only by an order of the President, passed after an address by **each House of Parliament** supported by a **majority of the total membership** of that House **and** by a **majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting**, presented in the same session, on the ground of **proved misbehaviour or incapacity**. Those are the only two grounds, and neither is defined.

The mechanics come from the **Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968**. A motion needs **100 members of the Lok Sabha** or **50 of the Rajya Sabha**. The presiding officer may admit or refuse it; if admitted, a three-member committee investigates, consisting of a Supreme Court judge, a High Court Chief Justice and a distinguished jurist. Only if the committee finds the charge proved does the motion go to a vote.

The attempts are the case law. **Justice V. Ramaswami** faced a motion in 1993 after a committee found charges proved; the Lok Sabha vote failed when the ruling party abstained. **Justice Soumitra Sen** was removed by a Rajya Sabha vote in 2011 but resigned before the Lok Sabha could take it up. **Justice Yashwant Varma** faced motions in 2025 after cash was found at his residence. The rule that a judge may resign before the second House votes is why the count stays at zero.

topics.title: India passes Japan to become the fourth largest economy
topics.hook: Fourth by the size of the pie and about one hundred and forty-first by the size of the slice.
topics.story:
India's **nominal GDP** reached about **$4.18 trillion**, moving it past Japan into **fourth place** behind the United States, China and Germany. The **World Bank** raised its growth forecast for the financial year to **7.2%**, citing softer food prices and better labour force participation.

Two measures are in play and they rank countries differently. **Nominal GDP** converts output at market exchange rates and is the one that produces this headline. **Purchasing power parity** adjusts for what money actually buys locally, and on that basis India has been **third** behind China and the United States for over a decade. Neither says anything about individuals: **per capita** income in nominal terms is around **$2,900**, which places India below the world average and outside the top hundred and thirty.

The composition has been unusual for a country at this stage. **Services** contribute roughly **55%** of gross value added and **industry** about 27%, while **agriculture** contributes around **18%** but still employs close to **45%** of the workforce. That gap between agriculture's share of output and of employment is the central structural problem, and it is what the phrase premature deindustrialisation points at.

Banking numbers were unusually good in the same month: **gross non-performing assets** fell to about **2.1%**, the lowest in more than a decade, against a peak above 11% in 2018 that followed the asset quality review.

topics.hook: India promised to get half its electricity capacity from non-fossil sources by 2030 and arrived early.
topics.story:
Installed renewable capacity reached about **254 GW**, and **non-fossil sources** crossed **50%** of India's total installed generating capacity, ahead of the 2030 target India set for itself.

The commitment comes from the **Panchamrit** pledges announced at **COP26 in Glasgow in 2021**: 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030, half of energy requirements from renewables, a billion tonnes cut in projected emissions, a 45% reduction in emissions intensity of GDP from 2005 levels, and **net zero by 2070**. These were folded into India's updated **Nationally Determined Contribution** under the **Paris Agreement**.

Capacity is not generation. Solar and wind run at much lower capacity factors than coal, so non-fossil sources supply well under half the electricity actually generated, and coal still carries about three quarters of it. The gap is a storage and transmission problem, which is what the viability gap funding for battery storage and the **green energy corridors** are meant to close. India also leads the world on renewable energy employment, with about **1.3 million** jobs across solar and hydropower.

topics.title: The G4 propose a Council of twenty-six
topics.hook: Every proposal to expand the Security Council has to be approved by the five countries whose relative power it would reduce.
topics.story:
The **G4** — India, Brazil, Germany and Japan — proposed expanding the Security Council to **25 or 26 members**, with **six new permanent seats** and four or five additional non-permanent ones, and offered to defer the question of the **veto** for the new permanent members for fifteen years.

The obstacle is structural. Amending the Charter requires a two-thirds vote in the General Assembly **and** ratification by two-thirds of members **including all five permanent members**, so any one of them can stop it. **Uniting for Consensus**, sometimes called the Coffee Club and led by Italy with Pakistan, Argentina, South Korea and others, opposes new permanent seats altogether and would add only elected members. The **African Union** presses the **Ezulwini Consensus**, which demands two permanent African seats with full veto rights.

India's case rests on population, on troop contributions to peacekeeping, on economic weight, and on eight terms as an elected member, the most recent in 2021 and 2022. Talks have run as **Intergovernmental Negotiations** since 2009 without a negotiating text that all sides accept, which is itself the standing complaint.

topics.title: Diego Garcia, the Chagos deal and the people who were removed
topics.hook: An advisory opinion said the islands should have gone with independence in 1968. The base is still there.
topics.story:
Attention returned to **Diego Garcia**, the American military base on the largest island of the **Chagos Archipelago**, held by Britain as the **British Indian Ocean Territory**.

Britain detached the archipelago from **Mauritius** in **1965**, three years before Mauritian independence, and between 1968 and 1973 removed the entire **Chagossian** population, mostly to Mauritius and the Seychelles, to make way for the base. The **International Court of Justice** held in a **2019 advisory opinion** that the detachment was unlawful because it broke up a colony before self-determination, and that Britain should end its administration as rapidly as possible. The **General Assembly** endorsed that by 116 votes to 6. An advisory opinion binds nobody, and Britain did not comply.

A **2024 agreement** transferred sovereignty over the archipelago to Mauritius while leasing Diego Garcia back for the base for an initial ninety-nine years. Chagossian groups have objected that they were not party to the negotiation and that the right of return to Diego Garcia itself remains excluded. India supported Mauritius throughout, which fits both its decolonisation position and its interest in the western Indian Ocean.

topics.title: India in the Arctic, and the sea route that is opening
topics.hook: A country with no Arctic coastline runs a research station there, because what happens on that ice decides the monsoon.
topics.story:
India expanded its Arctic engagement through fresh research missions, holding **observer status** on the **Arctic Council** since **2013**.

The Council was created by the **Ottawa Declaration of 1996** and has **eight member states** with territory above the Arctic Circle: Canada, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Russia, Sweden and the United States. Six organisations of indigenous peoples sit as **Permanent Participants**. India is one of thirteen observer states, alongside China, Japan and South Korea. India's station **Himadri**, at **Ny-Ålesund** in Svalbard, has operated since **2008**, and India's presence rests on the **Svalbard Treaty of 1920**, to which it has been a party since 1920 and which allows all signatories commercial and research access to the archipelago under Norwegian sovereignty.

The **Arctic Policy** released in 2022 sets out six pillars from science to connectivity. The scientific interest is direct: Arctic warming is running at roughly **twice the global average**, and changes in polar circulation and sea ice are linked to monsoon variability. The strategic interest is the **Northern Sea Route** along Russia's coast, which shortens the passage from East Asia to Europe substantially as ice retreats, and which India and Russia have discussed developing alongside the **Chennai-Vladivostok** maritime corridor.

topics.title: The carbon credit scheme widens to 208 industries
topics.hook: A domestic carbon price is worth paying because somebody else will otherwise collect it at their border.
topics.story:
India widened its **Carbon Credit Trading Scheme**, bringing **208 industrial entities** under a compliance mechanism that requires them to cut the **emission intensity** of their output against a benchmark, and to buy credits if they miss it.

The scheme was notified under the **Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022**, and is administered by the **Bureau of Energy Efficiency** with the Grid Controller of India as registry. It has a **compliance** side, where obligated entities must meet targets, and an **offset** side, where non-obligated entities can earn credits for voluntary reductions. It replaces the older **Perform, Achieve and Trade** scheme, which traded energy savings certificates rather than carbon.

The timing is not accidental. The European Union's **carbon border adjustment mechanism** entered its definitive phase in January 2026 and charges importers of steel, aluminium, cement, fertiliser, electricity and hydrogen for embedded emissions, with a deduction for any carbon price already paid at origin. A domestic price therefore keeps at home money that would otherwise be collected at the European border, which has turned an environmental instrument into a trade defence.

topics.title: Startup India at ten, and the IPO count
topics.hook: More new listings than any other country in the world, and most of the money raised went to companies nobody outside finance has heard of.
topics.story:
**Startup India**, launched in **January 2016**, completed a decade with about **2.09 lakh** recognised startups and more than **120 unicorns**, companies valued above a billion dollars. Around **45%** of recognised startups report at least one woman founder.

Recognition by the **Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade** brings a package: income tax exemption for three of the first ten years under **Section 80-IAC**, exemption from the so-called angel tax on share premium, self-certification on nine labour and three environmental laws, faster patent examination with an 80% fee rebate, and access to the **Fund of Funds for Startups** operated through SIDBI.

Separately, India ranked **first in the world by the number of initial public offerings**, with about **311 issues** raising roughly **₹1.7 trillion**. Listings are regulated by the **Securities and Exchange Board of India**, a statutory body under the SEBI Act 1992, which clears the offer document, and the shift of retail money into equity through systematic investment plans is what has kept the pipeline open.

topics.title: Gig workers strike over the ten-minute delivery model
topics.hook: The law finally named them in 2020, and then did not bring the law into force.
topics.story:
Delivery workers struck across several cities against **ten-minute delivery** targets, arguing that the model forces unsafe riding and that platform work still carries almost no social security.

The **Code on Social Security, 2020** was the first Indian statute to define a **gig worker**, a person who works outside a traditional employer-employee relationship, and a **platform worker**, one who accesses an organisation through an online platform to solve problems for payment. It provides for a **National Social Security Board** for these workers, for schemes covering life and disability cover, accident insurance, health and maternity benefit and old age protection, and for aggregators to contribute **1% to 2% of their turnover**, capped at 5% of what they pay workers.

The Code is one of four that consolidate twenty-nine older labour laws, alongside the Codes on **Wages**, on **Industrial Relations**, and on **Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions**. Implementation waited on state rules and central notification for years. **Rajasthan** passed its own platform workers' welfare law in 2023, and **Karnataka** followed, each creating a welfare board funded by a levy on transactions.

topics.title: The Piprahwa relics come home
topics.hook: Gems buried with the Buddha, dug up by a colonial landowner in 1898, and auctioned in Hong Kong in 2025.
topics.story:
The **Piprahwa relics** were displayed in New Delhi after their return, closing a repatriation dispute that had run through 2025.

They were excavated in **1898** at **Piprahwa** in Siddharthnagar district of Uttar Pradesh, near the site identified with **Kapilavastu**, by the estate manager **William Claxton Peppé**. A sandstone coffer held bone fragments, ash and about 1,800 gems, with an inscription in Brahmi recording the relics of the Buddha deposited by the Sakya clan. Most of the bone was given to the King of Siam; the gems stayed with the Peppé family. When a portion was put up for auction at **Sotheby's Hong Kong in May 2025**, the Ministry of Culture objected that they were **corporeal relics** rather than art, inalienable under Indian law and under the sensibilities of a living religion. The sale was withdrawn.

The governing statutes are the **Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972**, which controls export and requires registration, and the **Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958**, under which the Archaeological Survey of India works. Internationally the instrument is the **1970 UNESCO Convention** on illicit transfer of cultural property, to which India is a party.

passages.title: A doctrine two centuries old
passages.passage:
In a message to Congress in 1823 an American president told the European powers that the hemisphere was closed to further colonisation, that any attempt to extend their political system to it would be regarded as dangerous to American peace and safety, and that in return the United States would not interfere in European affairs or in existing European colonies. The statement was not a treaty and created no obligation on anyone. For decades it was largely aspirational, since the navy that would have enforced it did not exist and the Royal Navy, whose interest in open South American markets ran the same way, did the enforcing in practice.

Its meaning changed at the start of the twentieth century. A later president added that chronic wrongdoing by a state of the hemisphere might force the United States to exercise an international police power, which converted a warning aimed outward into a licence to intervene inward. That addition was invoked in the Caribbean repeatedly over the next thirty years. A successor administration disavowed intervention in the 1930s, and a secretary of state announced in 2013 that the era of the doctrine was over.

The vocabulary returned in early 2026, when American forces captured the Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and officials described the hemisphere in terms the 1823 message would have recognised. The legal question raised in response was narrower than the historical one. The prohibition on the use of force in the UN Charter admits of two exceptions, self-defence against an armed attack and authorisation by the Security Council, and neither was claimed in terms.

questions.q: The 1823 statement is known as:
questions.explain: The Monroe Doctrine, from President James Monroe's message to Congress.

questions.q: The early twentieth-century addition described in the third sentence of paragraph two is:
questions.explain: The Roosevelt Corollary asserted an international police power in the hemisphere.

questions.q: On the passage, the doctrine was enforced in practice in its early decades by:
questions.explain: The passage says the Royal Navy did the enforcing because British commercial interests ran the same way.

questions.q: The two exceptions to the prohibition on force under the UN Charter are:
options: Regional consent and Security Council authorisation
questions.explain: Article 51 self-defence and Chapter VII authorisation by the Security Council.

questions.q: Which of the following is most consistent with the passage?
options: The doctrine created binding obligations in international law
The doctrine was a unilateral policy statement
The doctrine was adopted by the Organization of American States
The doctrine was abandoned permanently in 1930s
questions.explain: The passage says it was not a treaty and created no obligation, and that its vocabulary returned in 2026.

passages.title: Reading health into a sentence
passages.passage:
A petition asked for a national policy requiring schools to provide sanitary products and functioning separate toilets, arguing that girls drop out when neither exists. The court could have disposed of it as a matter of administrative direction. It chose instead to locate the claim in the right to life, holding that menstrual health is part of the dignity that the article protects and that the state's obligation follows from the right rather than from any scheme.

The move follows a familiar pattern. The same article has been read to include a right to livelihood, to a clean environment, to shelter, to legal aid, to a speedy trial and to privacy, each time by reasoning that life means more than animal existence. Two directive principles were cited in support: one directing the state to raise the level of nutrition and the standard of public health, and one requiring provision for just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief. Directive principles are not enforceable by any court, but the judgment used them as they have long been used, to give content to a fundamental right rather than to create a separate claim.

The order directed the framing of a uniform national policy, periodic reporting by states, and audits of school sanitation. Whether that produces toilets is a separate question from whether it produces a right, and the court acknowledged as much by retaining the matter for compliance.

passages.title: Cutting into growth
passages.passage:
The committee that sets the policy rate has six members, and it cut by a quarter point at its first meeting of the year on the ground that inflation had settled inside the band while growth was running ahead of the earlier estimate. The rate it sets is the one at which the central bank lends overnight to commercial banks against government securities, and it is the anchor from which the rest of the corridor is drawn: a facility at which banks may borrow at a higher rate against their statutory holdings sits above it, and the rate at which the bank absorbs surplus liquidity sits below.

Transmission is the difficulty. A cut takes effect immediately on loans priced against an external benchmark, since most floating-rate retail loans have been required since 2019 to be linked to the policy rate or a treasury yield rather than to a bank's own cost of funds. It takes much longer on deposits and on older loans, so the effect on lending overall arrives over quarters rather than weeks.

Alongside the rate the committee announces a stance, which signals direction rather than action. The stance had been shifted to neutral before this meeting, which left room to move either way. The vote was not unanimous, and the minutes published a fortnight later showed one member arguing that the growth estimate was preliminary and might be revised.

passages.title: Chairing a widened table
passages.passage:
The grouping began as an acronym coined by a bank economist in 2001 to describe four large economies expected to dominate growth. The four began meeting as a bloc in 2009 and added a fifth member the following year, which changed the acronym. For more than a decade the membership stayed there. Expansion in 2024 and after brought in several more states, most of them large energy producers or populous middle powers, and turned a compact caucus into something looser.

Its most concrete institution is a development bank headquartered in Shanghai, established by treaty in 2014 and open to membership beyond the original five. Alongside it sits a currency reserve arrangement of the same vintage, intended as a swap line for members facing balance of payments pressure. Neither has displaced the institutions created at Bretton Woods, and the bank lends a fraction of what the older ones do, but both were founded on the argument that voting power in those institutions had not kept pace with the distribution of world output.

India took the rotating chair for 2026 and named its priorities as reformed multilateralism, counter-terrorism, digital public infrastructure and climate finance. The recurring internal difficulty is that the members disagree on the point of the exercise: some treat it as a vehicle for reforming existing institutions and others as an alternative to them, and proposals for a common currency have been floated by one member and quietly declined by others.

passages.title: The sanction question
passages.passage:
Before a public servant can be prosecuted for an offence connected to the discharge of official duty, the statute requires the previous approval of the authority competent to remove that person from office. The purpose is to shield honest officials from vexatious prosecution, and the protection is not a formality: a prosecution launched without it is void, and the defect cannot be cured by obtaining approval later.

Two questions recur. The first is whether the requirement survives after the official has left the post. An amendment in 2018 extended the protection to former public servants for acts done while in office, reversing an earlier line of authority. The second is what happens when the approving authority is itself the accused's superior in a matter where the superior has an interest, and here the court has held that a deemed refusal after three months does not authorise prosecution, since the statute fixes a period for decision rather than a period after which consent is presumed.

A two-judge bench divided in January 2026 on whether the requirement applies where the alleged act, though committed by a public servant, could not by any stretch form part of official duty. One judge held that the protection attaches to the office and must be tested at the threshold. The other held that an act incapable of being an official duty falls outside the section altogether, so no approval is needed and the trial may proceed. The matter goes to a larger bench.
